opus-5.5.text:
I think it's closer than people might assume, but it's not all the way there yet, and I'd be honest about where the gap is.

If you take The Bitter Lesson seriously, the claim is that general methods that scale with computation and data eventually win over methods that bake in human knowledge. Classical task and motion planning is almost the poster child for the opposite: hand-written symbolic operators, carefully designed predicates, geometric constraints, samplers that someone tuned by hand. It works beautifully in the domains it was designed for, and then it's brittle the moment you step outside them.

What we've been trying to do with generative TAMP is keep the part of the structure that I think is genuinely useful, which is the idea of composing solutions, reasoning over long horizons, and satisfying constraints, while replacing the hand-engineered pieces with learned generative models. So instead of writing a sampler for a grasp or a placement, you learn a distribution over those things from data, say with a diffusion model, and then compose those learned models at inference time to solve problems you never saw during training. That part, I'd argue, is very much in the spirit of The Bitter Lesson. The more data and compute you throw at those components, the better they get, and you're not capping performance with a human's idea of what a good grasp looks like.

Where we're still not fully there is the compositional scaffolding itself. We still impose some structure: how skills or constraints get factored, what the interfaces between them look like, how the search or the inference procedure is organized. Someone could reasonably say that's human knowledge sneaking back in. And I think that's a fair critique.

My view is that structure isn't the enemy per se. The question is whether the structure scales or whether it becomes a bottleneck. Compositionality is something I believe is fundamental, because the world is combinatorial and you will never collect data for every combination of objects, tasks, and environments. So some way of recombining what you've learned is necessary for generalization. The bet is that the right kind of structure, very minimal, very general, actually lets you get more out of data and compute rather than less.

So if I were to put it on a spectrum, I'd say generative TAMP is maybe halfway. The local models are learned and scale nicely. The long-term direction is to make the compositional structure itself learned or emergent, so that the system discovers how to break problems down instead of us telling it. Whether that comes from large pretrained models, from better inference-time compute, or from something we haven't thought of yet, I think that's the interesting open question, and honestly one of the things I'm most excited about.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, honestly, because it cuts right to the tension in my own work.

So The Bitter Lesson, as Rich Sutton framed it, says that approaches which lean on general methods plus compute and data eventually beat approaches that bake in human knowledge about how the problem is structured. And task and motion planning is, almost by definition, the field that bakes in the most structure. You have symbolic predicates, you have hand-designed operators, you have a geometric planner underneath, and you have a search procedure that stitches them together. It's a beautiful piece of engineering, but it's a monument to human priors.

Where I'd say we are right now is somewhere in the middle, and I'd put it this way: the lesson is being learned one layer at a time, from the bottom up. Learned motion primitives replaced hand-tuned controllers. Then we started learning samplers for the geometric side, learning where to grasp, where to place, so the planner doesn't flail around. Then people started learning the symbolic layer itself, or generating plans directly with sequence models or diffusion models over trajectories. Every one of those steps was the field saying, okay, this piece we thought required human structure actually gets better when you learn it.

But I don't think we've fully conformed, and I'd be a little skeptical of anyone who says we have. The honest reason is data. The Bitter Lesson has an implicit precondition, which is that compute and data scale. In language and vision that's basically true. In robotics, especially for long-horizon manipulation, the data is still scarce, expensive, and embodiment-specific. So when people hold onto structure, say a planner that enforces feasibility, or a factored representation that lets you generalize across object counts, they're often not being stubborn about priors. They're compensating for a data regime where the pure end-to-end approach just doesn't have enough signal to learn long-horizon reasoning on its own.

The thing I find interesting is that the structure that survives is changing character. It's less "here are the symbols and the rules," and more "here's an inductive bias about compositionality, or a verification loop that catches when the model hallucinates an infeasible plan." Those feel less like hand-coded knowledge and more like scaffolding that a learned system can grow into and eventually outgrow. I'd actually argue the most Bitter-Lesson-compatible thing you can do right now is to design structure that you fully expect to be deleted in three years.

So if you asked me to put a number on it, I'd say the geometric and skill-level pieces are mostly there. The long-horizon task-level reasoning is maybe halfway, and the part that will fall last is reliability, actually getting the thing to succeed on the twentieth step in a row, because that's where the search-and-verify machinery still earns its keep. My bet is that it does eventually go the way of everything else, but the timeline is gated on data collection and simulation at a scale we don't have yet, not on anyone's clever architecture.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re moving in that direction, but we’re not quite there yet. The way I interpret the Bitter Lesson is that methods that can keep benefiting from more computation and more data tend to win over methods where we hand-engineer a lot of the structure.

Task and motion planning traditionally has a lot of that engineered structure. We specify the actions, their preconditions, their effects, and then connect that symbolic description to a motion planner. That’s powerful, but there’s a lot of human effort involved in defining what the robot can do.

Generative models offer a way to learn some of that structure from data. But calling something generative doesn’t automatically mean it conforms to the Bitter Lesson. If it still depends on a carefully designed representation for every new task, then we haven’t really removed that bottleneck.

I also wouldn’t interpret the lesson as saying we should get rid of planning. Search is itself a way to benefit from more compute. The interesting direction is to learn models that propose useful actions or motions, and then use planning to check them and explore alternatives. The question is whether that whole system keeps improving as we scale it, without us having to redesign it for each new problem. I think that’s the direction, but I wouldn’t say we’ve demonstrated it convincingly yet.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re moving in that direction, but I wouldn’t say we’re there yet. The Bitter Lesson, as I understand it, is that methods that can keep benefiting from more computation and more data eventually outperform approaches built around a lot of human knowledge. In task and motion planning, we still put a tremendous amount of structure into the system: what the actions are, how we represent the world, how we break a task into pieces.

Generative models offer a way to learn some of that structure. Instead of manually specifying every possible strategy, you can learn a distribution of useful behaviors and use that to guide planning. But generating something that looks plausible is different from generating a plan that actually works when the robot executes it. You still need to deal with physical constraints, uncertainty, and recovery when something goes wrong.

So I think the key question is whether those learned components keep improving as we scale the data and computation, and whether that improvement translates into success on new tasks. Using a generative model doesn’t automatically mean you’ve embraced the Bitter Lesson. The stronger version would be a system that can discover better strategies through experience and search, without us continually redesigning its abstractions. That’s the direction I’m excited about, but there’s still a gap.
